title: What is competency-based training?
description: Competency-based training (CBT) trains and assesses people against defined workplace standards, not hours. How it works, with a worked example.
shortAnswer: A competency-based training (CBT) system is an approach in which learners are trained and assessed against defined workplace standards, and are judged competent when they can show they meet those standards, rather than when they have spent a set amount of time in a course. National vocational systems such as Australia's are built on this model, using published units of competency as the standards.
keyTakeaways: Competency-based training focuses on what a person can do at the workplace standard, not on hours of attendance or a ranked grade.
In national vocational systems, the standards are published occupational standards, such as the units of competency in nationally endorsed training packages listed on training.gov.au.
Assessment results are typically competent or not yet competent, supported by evidence against the unit's requirements.
Regulated training providers must also meet formal assessment rules, such as the principles of assessment and rules of evidence in the 2025 Standards for RTOs.

blocks.text: Competency-based training works by starting from a defined standard of workplace performance, teaching toward it, and then collecting evidence that the learner meets it. The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) [Training Package Organizing Framework](https://www.dewr.gov.au/download/16680/training-package-organising-framework-effective-1-july-2025/39042/training-package-organising-framework/pdf) states that training packages "focus on what is expected of a competent individual in the workplace as an outcome of learning, rather than focussing on the learning process itself."

items: **Define the standard.** A unit of competency, or an internal [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework), describes the task, the performance criteria and the knowledge required.
**Recognize what the learner already has.** [Recognition of prior learning](/glossary/recognition-of-prior-learning) can credit existing competence so training time is not wasted.
**Train to the gap.** Instruction and practice target the parts of the standard the learner cannot yet meet.
**Assess against the standard.** A [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) gathers performance and knowledge evidence.
**Record the decision.** The learner is judged competent or not yet competent, with the evidence retained.

sections.heading: How is competency-based training used in national vocational systems?

blocks.text: Competency-based training is the basis of many national vocational systems. Australia's nationally recognized vocational education and training (VET) system is one example. Training packages, developed by Jobs and Skills Councils and published on [training.gov.au](https://training.gov.au), contain units of competency and qualifications aligned to the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF). Registered Training Organisations (RTOs) deliver and assess them, and the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) is the national VET regulator.

The [2025 Standards for RTOs](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs), which took effect on July 1, 2025, set the quality bar. ASQA's [assessment practice guide](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/practice-guides/quality-area-1-training-and-assessment/assessment-practice-guide) states that Standard 1.4 requires assessment to follow the principles of fairness, flexibility, validity and reliability, and assessor judgments to meet the rules of evidence: validity, sufficiency, authenticity and currency. The details are covered in [Standards for RTOs 2025: training and assessment](/regulations/standards-for-rtos-2025-training-and-assessment).

Employers outside the VET system use the same model for internal programs, particularly in safety critical and regulated roles, where the question a regulator asks is whether the worker can do the task safely, not whether they attended a session.

sections.heading: What does competency-based training look like for one task?

blocks.text: Illustrative example: a logistics business uses nationally endorsed units, delivered through an RTO, for general equipment operation. For site specific tasks that no national unit covers, such as its own dangerous goods segregation rules, it writes an internal competency with the same structure.

items: **Standard:** segregates incompatible dangerous goods classes according to the site segregation chart.
**Performance evidence:** correctly segregates three mixed loads under observation.
**Knowledge evidence:** explains the segregation chart and the incident reporting step.
**Result:** competent, with observation checklist and knowledge responses retained; a learner who errs on one load is not yet competent and receives targeted practice.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures internal competencies the way the VET system structures units: requirement, performance evidence and knowledge evidence, each linked to a source. Training content and assessments are then generated against that structure rather than written first.

faqs.q: Is competency-based training the same as nationally recognized training?
faqs.a: No. In Australia's VET system, for example, nationally recognized training is competency-based, but not all competency-based training is nationally recognized. Only a Registered Training Organisation can issue qualifications or statements of attainment for units on training.gov.au. Employers can run their own competency-based programs, but those do not produce nationally recognized credentials.

faqs.q: Why are results competent or not yet competent rather than grades?
faqs.a: Because the question is whether the learner meets the workplace standard. A graded scale implies degrees of passing, but in competency-based training a person either meets the standard with sufficient evidence or does not yet meet it. Some providers add graded feedback, but the competency decision itself is binary.

faqs.q: Does competency-based training still have a minimum duration?
faqs.a: Competency is not granted for time served, but time still matters. ASQA expects providers to structure and pace training so learners have sufficient time for instruction, practice, feedback and assessment, and to establish the amount of training needed to reach an industry standard.

faqs.q: Can competency-based training be used for compliance topics?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is often a better fit than completion based e-learning. Writing the compliance obligation as a performance standard, such as correctly handling a scenario, gives evidence that people can apply the rule, which is closer to what regulators test after an incident.
